analysis.one_liner: Writes strict federal limits on PFAS 'forever chemicals' in drinking water into law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced June 26, 2025 with a Republican lead sponsor and 15 cosponsors, has sat without any committee vote or floor action since it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill takes the EPA's 2024 rule setting enforceable limits on PFAS — manmade 'forever chemicals' linked to cancer and other health harms — in public drinking water and makes it a statute. That means a future administration could not simply rescind or weaken the limits; Congress would have to act to change them. The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100 million people served by water systems that would have to filter PFAS down to the strict limits, plus communities near PFAS plants, military bases, and contaminated sites whose water currently exceeds the limits. Households would face lower long-term exposure to chemicals linked to cancer, liver and thyroid problems, and developmental harm in children.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the force of law to the EPA's final PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation as it stood on June 25, 2024, making the limits a statute rather than a regulation that an administration could rewrite. [S2]
The underlying rule sets enforceable, legally binding maximum limits for PFAS in public drinking water nationwide, which water systems must treat down to. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Water utilities bear the cost of installing filtration and testing to meet the limits, and those costs are largely passed to customers through water bills. Chemical manufacturers face greater liability and cleanup exposure because the standard is locked in as law.

drawbacks.text: Meeting the limits requires new treatment and monitoring at water systems, and small and rural utilities with thin budgets would face the steepest per-household costs, likely passed on in water bills. [S2]

Codifying the rule as it stood on a single date freezes one scientific snapshot into law; if better data later justified different limits in either direction, only Congress could change them, rather than EPA scientists through normal rulemaking. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of removing 'forever chemicals' from drinking water is large and falls on the public broadly; the compliance cost is real and falls on utilities and ratepayers, hardest on small systems. The main design weakness is that it fixes one version of the rule in statute, trading regulatory flexibility for durability against rollback.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled a hearing, a markup, or a vote on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 26, 2025, joined by Rep. Debbie Dingell, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S1] [S4]
Fifteen members cosponsored the bill, 14 Democrats and 1 Republican, giving it bipartisan but modest support. [S3]
No further action has been taken since the referral: no committee vote, no floor vote. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's position has changed: the 2024 PFAS rule remains an ordinary regulation rather than a law, which benefits chemical manufacturers and water utilities seeking flexibility or relief from its limits. Communities waiting for enforceable cleanup of their drinking water have gained nothing yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; status quo persists

for.name: Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to codify the EPA's PFAS drinking water rule into law and referred it to Energy and Commerce. [S1] [S4]

for.name: Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Joined Fitzpatrick in introducing the bill. [S2]

for.name: 14 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including 14 Democrats and one Republican. [S3]

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing, markup, or vote on the bill since it was referred on June 26, 2025. [S4]

against.name: EPA under the Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Announced in 2025 that it would keep limits for the two most notorious PFAS but reconsider, extend deadlines for, and rescind parts of the 2024 rule for other PFAS compounds — the rollback this bill is designed to prevent.

against.name: Chemical manufacturers and water utilities
against.role: PFAS producers and regulated water systems
against.what_they_did: Sought relief from the 2024 rule's compliance deadlines and liability exposure through litigation, settlement negotiations, and regulatory petitions.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican led the bill and 14 of its 15 cosponsors are Democrats, so support crosses party lines, though it leans Democratic. [S3]

industries.note: The companies that made the chemicals now contaminating water supplies would face a permanent, court-enforceable standard and greater liability. The bill's whole purpose is to stop their preferred path, which is weakening the rule through the EPA.
Utilities must pay billions for filtration, monitoring, and infrastructure to meet the limits, costs passed to ratepayers. Their product, safer water, is what the public gets in exchange.
A binding national standard creates demand for carbon filtration, reverse osmosis, and testing services to bring systems into compliance.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Energy and Commerce in the first months of a Congress rarely reach the floor unless leadership prioritizes them, and this one has no scheduled action. A codification bill like this is more likely to move, if at all, as part of a broader PFAS or water infrastructure package, or if public pressure over contamination grows.
